Sealed Bids

AlgorithmsLogicFractions
Game: Everyone secretly says what each item is worth to them. Each item goes to the person who bid the most, and money is paid to make things fair. There is nothing to win — see how the money works out.
How to play: Click the left or right half of a bid to change it, or use arrow keys. Change the number of bidders or items, or press New bids for a fresh table.

A W marks the winning bid in each row. Tap the left half of a bid to lower it, the right half to raise it; arrow keys work too. A wide table slides sideways.

Look for the math

Suppose friends are sharing several things but value them differently. The method of sealed bids hands every item to whoever wants it most, then uses cash so that everyone ends up with what they think is a fair share.

Who gets each item

Look down an item's row: the largest bid wins it, and a W marks that cell. If two people tie, the applet flips a coin, so the same tie can go to different bidders on different runs. With three equal bids the last bidder wins half the time, because each later coin flip can take the lead from the one before.

What is a fair share?

Each bidder's fair share is the average of the bids they made, not the average of everyone's bids. If Amelia bid 9, 4 and 2, her total is 15 and, with three bidders, her fair share is 5. Adding all the fair shares adds up to all the bids divided by the number of bidders.

Paying and receiving

The Owe(s/d) row is what each bidder received minus their fair share. A positive amount means they must pay; a negative one means they should be paid. The amounts left over cannot add up to a negative number: for every item, the highest bid is at least the average of the bids on that item, so the total received is at least the total of the fair shares.

Splitting the leftovers

The cash left over is shared equally. A bidder's final cash is the negative of what they owe, plus their equal slice of the surplus, so the payments and receipts cancel exactly: the Cash column adds up to zero. The applet prints only two decimal places, so the printed amounts may be a cent away from zero. Change one bid and you will see both columns move, but the last row balances again.

What was checked

The logic test compares the whole calculation with a second transcription of the applet's own method on about 266,000 small bid tables, and on tables at the option limits: 2 to 26 bidders and 1 to 15 items, with bids from 0 to 1000. It checks that winners really bid the most, that the surplus is never negative and that the cash balances. It also checks the applet's odd number formatting: a small negative such as -0.05 is printed as -.0-, and half a unit is printed as .50 with no leading zero. The page keeps the applet's numbers as they are.

Give two bidders identical bids for one item, press New bids a few times, and watch the W jump between them.
